Full article: The contradictions of democratization by force: the case of Iraq

# The contradictions of democratization by force: the case of Iraq

David Beetham Correspondence dbeetham@mighty-micro.co.uk 

 Pages 443-454 | Received 15 Jan 2009, Published online: 27 May 2009

- Preliminary objections
- The contradictions of democratization through invasion
- Potential counter-examples
- Consequences for democracy at home
- Note on contributor
- Footnotes
- References

## Abstract

The article uses the Iraq example to show that the project of imposing democracy from outside by force is inherently contradictory and likely to fail, for reasons that go beyond the particular circumstances of the country or the Middle East. The paper then reviews a number of historical cases that have been supposed to show that democracy can result from armed invasion, and concludes that this was only so because in no case was imposing democracy the prime purpose of an invasion. Finally, it draws attention to the consequences for the quality of democracy at home in the countries most responsible for seeking to export democracy by force of arms.

In the previous issue of Democratization Laurence Whitehead argued that Iraq constituted a ‘pivotal case’ for democratization theory, on the grounds that it exposed to clear view the ‘dark side’ that had always existed, insufficiently acknowledged, in the practice of democracy promotion. Footnote 1 This article argues that Iraq is a ‘pivotal case’ in an even more fundamental sense, in exemplifying the contradictions inherent in the project of imposing democracy by force. As John Stuart Mill commented a century and a half ago:

If it were possible for the people to be well governed in spite of themselves, their good government would last no longer than the freedom of a people usually lasts who have been liberated by foreign arms without their own cooperation. Footnote 2 

The first part of the article will explore the contradictions inherent in what Whitehead terms ‘coercive democratization’, and why it is likely to fail. The second part will briefly examine some potential counter-examples where the external invasion of a country by another has led to regime change and democratization, and I will argue that, properly understood, they are not counter-examples at all. In the third and final part I will assess the impact of the invasion of Iraq on democracy in the countries that were responsible for the invasion.

## Preliminary objections

Before I begin I need to dispose of some preliminary objections to drawing any general conclusion from Iraq about the likely failure of forcible democratic imposition. These objections take one of three forms.

(1) The first objection is that the invasion by the United States and the United Kingdom was not directed at democratization at all, but at the more limited goal of removing Saddam's weapons of mass destruction, to which ‘regime change’ was simply the means. Certainly the supposed presence of weapons of mass destruction was the ostensible casus belli, but only because ‘for bureaucratic reasons … it was the one reason everyone could agree on’, Footnote 3 and the only one that could plausibly be put before the United Nations following Tony Blair's insistence on Security Council approval. Yet we know that the intelligence ‘facts had to be fitted round the policy’, and that the involvement of the United Nations in the abortive inspection regime was intended to legitimate, rather than prevent, a war that had already been decided upon on other grounds. Footnote 4 As Jonathan Powell, Tony Blair's chief of staff, admitted later, ‘We should have been clear we were removing Saddam because he was a ruthless dictator suppressing his people. But the lawyers said there was no legal basis for proceeding on these grounds’. Footnote 5 

There is now plentiful evidence that the neo-conservative group in the US administration had long planned forcible regime change in Iraq, and that the events of 9/11 enabled them to achieve dominance over other elements within the administration. Footnote 6 They saw forcible regime change in Iraq as the key to a reconfiguration of the whole Middle East, both through a dramatic demonstration of US power and through the installation of a democratic regime in Iraq. This regime would serve a number of purposes: it would be amenable to US interests, particularly its oil security; it would act as a catalyst for democratization across the whole region through its ‘demonstration effects’; and it would reduce the threat to Israel's security, since democracies supposedly do not go to war against other democracies, or support international terrorism. Footnote 7 Moreover, once weapons of mass destruction were shown not to have existed, democratization moved centre-stage as the explicit justification for the invasion. We can only conclude that this is an example of intentional democratization by force.

(2) A second objection is that it is far too soon to judge the project of forcible democratization in Iraq to have been a failure, however poorly the country currently performs against international criteria for democracy. As Tony Blair has frequently claimed, democratization is a long drawn out process, and only ‘history’ will be able to judge whether the invasion has been a success or failure. Some have even taken the recent peaceful provincial elections of January 2009 as evidence that ‘history’ has already delivered its verdict. Under the headline ‘Democratic Dawn in Iraq’, William Shawcross writes that ‘Iraq may yet even become a model for democratic change in other Arab countries. If so, who deserves some credit? The much maligned President Bush. And Tony Blair’. Footnote 8 A more cautious assessment would be one of scepticism that this is any different from the previous false dawns and abortive ‘turning points’ that have been so confidently discovered in Iraq's development since 2003.

One thing, however, can be said with some certainty. Whatever the future brings, and whatever form of regime emerges over time, the example of the invasion and occupation of Iraq could never serve to support any future attempt at forcible democratization, given the enormous costs it has imposed on all involved, not least on the Iraqi people themselves. A reasoned estimate of these includes hundreds of thousands of Iraqis killed or wounded, two million displaced internally and over two million refugees in other countries. Footnote 9 Such costs have served to discredit such a project for the indefinite future, and to remove the category of enforced democratization from the agenda of possible transitions to democracy. Far from offering a model, therefore, Iraq constitutes rather a dire warning.

(3) A further objection holds that no general conclusions can be drawn from Iraq about the feasibility of imposed democratization, because the failures were mistakes of implementation, not of the original conception itself; so we cannot conclude anything more general from it. This is a view that is widely held in Washington. It is also the view of even such an eminent scholar as Larry Diamond in his book with the revealing title Squandered Victory: The American Occupation and the Bungled Effort to Bring Democracy to Iraq. The title of course implies that there was a way for the effort not to have been ‘bungled’. In Chapter 10 Diamond presents a list of errors made in the course of the invasion and its aftermath, through which the democratization project (in which he took part himself) came to be undermined. Footnote 10 

This view is disingenuous, because it ignores the fact that the errors of implementation were not contingent mistakes, but were inscribed in the nature of the project and its authors from the outset. Their mindset was characterized by two elements: an extraordinary belief in large-scale social engineering, provided it takes place abroad; and a highly simplified view of social and political processes. Both were evident in the recipes for economic liberalization in Russia and elsewhere after 1990, where it was believed that, if you removed the state from the economy, a fully-fledged market system would emerge, regardless of any institutional conditions or supports. Both were also evident in the project for democratization in Iraq: remove an oppressive state and democracy will spring up of its own accord, as if it were a ‘default position’ to which societies will gravitate once the source of their oppression is removed. To say that the Iraq project failed through errors of implementation is to wish that different authors had been in charge; for example, those who would have listened to independent experts on Iraq and the region rather than marginalizing them. But these would have been ones who would most probably never have embarked on the project in the first place.

One reason why they might not have lies in the specific regional context. Paul Rogers, in his book Why We're Losing the War on Terror, makes short shrift of the idea that the Iraq invasion was viable in principle, but only the execution was lacking:

The problem with this outlook, which is likely to endure in Washington whatever the eventual outcome in Iraq, is that it is so fundamentally flawed as to be delusional … The Iraq operation was a delusion because it presumed that a foreign power could simply terminate a regime in a major Arab state and replace it with an acceptable regime of its own choosing. Moreover, this was a foreign power that was closely linked to Israel, a relationship that had an enduring negative resonance across the region. Operation Enduring Freedom was flawed from the outset. Footnote 11 

I agree with Paul Rogers' conclusion, but for reasons that go beyond the particular regional context. My argument is that democratization through invasion, or forcible democratization, is intrinsically flawed and self-contradictory, for reasons independent of any regional context, as I will set out in the next section.

## The contradictions of democratization through invasion

There are two main reasons why democratization through invasion is intrinsically flawed and self-contradictory: the first stems from the democratic logic of self-determination; the second from a consideration of democracy's preconditions.

### The logic of self-determination

If the basic idea of democracy is that of self-determination – that a people should determine their own affairs – then it is self-contradictory to try to initiate that through a violation of their self-determination by a forcible invasion and occupation, compelling them ‘to be free’. Democracy shares with sovereignty the core idea of popular self-determination, of which one is the internal, the other the external, expression. The fact that the latter does not guarantee the former, as we all know, does not excuse us ignoring the intrinsic connection between them. It is no accident that the age of democracy in the second half of the twentieth century was also the age of anti-imperialism, and the establishment of self-governing states from former empires through popular struggle. With some exaggeration, Michael Mann writes that ‘nationalism is now the world's dominant ideology … There is no widespread ideology legitimizing anyone else ruling over a nation-state. Since only “the people” should rule, anti-imperialism is rampant across the world’. Footnote 12 

This normative connection between democracy and the principle of national self-government is overlooked by those who argue either that state sovereignty is an outmoded legal category or that it should be trumped by the principle of democracy and human rights, where the latter are violated by a domestic oppressor. This argument formed a post hoc justification for the Iraq invasion by those who have come to be known as ‘liberal imperialists’ or ‘Wilsonians in boots’.
